title: Le Nozze di Figaro
facts: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 528th Le Nozze di Figaro.
Host Julia Bullock debuted at the Met in 2024, in El Niño by John Adams, who calls her his muse.
Joana Mallwitz makes her Met debut with this Figaro. Her first professional conducting job came at six hours’ notice.
At the 1786 premiere, the audience demanded encores of five numbers. On 8 May, seven.
Richard Eyre’s staging opened the Met’s 2014–15 season, with James Levine conducting.
It was Mozart who picked Beaumarchais’s play. Da Ponte turned it into a libretto in six weeks.
Servant versus count: Beaumarchais’s play, with its frank class conflict, was at first banned in Vienna.
Basilio’s phrase “Così fan tutte le belle” here later turned up in the overture to Mozart’s Così fan tutte.
A C-major military march: the tune mimics a bugle on natural harmonics, and the horns join in.
Mozart quoted this tune in Don Giovanni, where Leporello sighs: “Now that tune I know too well.”
“Porgi, amor” reuses the motif that opens Mozart’s early bassoon concerto.
Federica Lombardi, our Countess, debuted at the Met in 2019 as Donna Elvira; at Covent Garden, as this Countess.
In 1789 Mozart replaced this aria for a new Susanna. The Met used his replacements in 1998, with Cecilia Bartoli.
The Act II finale starts here: over 900 bars of continuous music, one of Mozart’s longest uninterrupted stretches.
Count the voices: eight of the opera’s 11 characters pile in, climaxing in a seven- and eight-voice tutti.
“Dove sono” begins like the Agnus Dei of Mozart’s Coronation Mass, moved from F major to C major.
Oboes and bassoons fill the Countess’s rests with expressive motifs, which she later picks up.
Today “Dove sono” came before this sextet. Mozart’s score puts it after; two scholars argued this order is more logical.
The letter duet: B-flat major, 6/8, oboe and bassoon. The Countess dictates; Susanna repeats each line as she writes.
In this production, the two peasant girls’ music is sung by Barbarina and Cherubino.
Da Ponte swapped Figaro’s climactic speech against inherited nobility for an equally angry aria against unfaithful wives.
Hear the two horns playing together? That’s Mozart’s joke for cuckoldry. Verdi borrowed it in Falstaff.
Olga Kulchynska, our Susanna, learned three days ahead she’d sing the Bolshoi premiere of The Tsar’s Bride.
Listen for the Count’s plea, “Contessa, perdono!” Her reply: “I am kinder, and I say yes.”
